topic: Navigation systems: VOR, DME, ILS, GPS and RNAV

notes.front: What is a nondirectional radio beacon (NDB)?
notes.back: A low or medium frequency beacon whose signals let a suitably equipped aircraft find bearings to it and home on it.
notes.explanation: The aircraft uses an ADF to point at the beacon; the beacon itself sends the same signal in every direction.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-2 “Nondirectional Radio Beacon (NDB)”
notes.evidence: A low or medium frequency radio beacon transmits nondirectional signals whereby the pilot of an aircraft properly equipped can determine bearings and “home” on the station.
notes.example: Like a lighthouse that shines equally all round, where the ship’s own direction-finder does the work of saying which way it lies.

notes.front: What is the localizer (LOC) of an ILS?
notes.back: The ILS transmitter that gives course guidance to the runway centreline.
notes.explanation: Its approach course is the front course, used together with the glide slope and marker beacons.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: Signals provide the pilot with course guidance to the runway centerline.
notes.example: Like the painted centre line on a motorway slip road, but made of radio waves and extending miles out from the runway.

notes.front: What is the glide slope (GS) of an ILS?
notes.back: The ILS transmitter that gives vertical (descent) guidance along the localizer front course.
notes.explanation: The glide path is the part of the glide slope that intersects the localizer.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: radiates its signals in the direction of the localizer front course. The term “glide path” means that portion of the glide slope that intersects the localizer.
notes.example: Like the handrail on a ramp that tells you how steeply to go down, while the localizer tells you which way.

notes.front: What is the localizer back course?
notes.back: The localizer course along the extended runway centreline on the opposite side from the front course.
notes.explanation: It can only be used for an approach where a back course procedure is published and ATC authorises it.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: The course line along the extended centerline of a runway, in the opposite direction to the front course is called the back course.
notes.example: Like the back of a torch beam: the same light, but shining out behind you.

notes.front: What is a localizer-type directional aid (LDA)?
notes.back: A facility of comparable use and accuracy to a localizer, but not part of a complete ILS and not aligned with the runway.
notes.explanation: Because its course is not aligned with the runway, more manoeuvring is needed than on an ILS.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: The LDA is of comparable use and accuracy to a localizer but is not part of a complete ILS.
notes.example: Like a localizer whose beam points at the runway from an angle, so you finish with a turn to line up.

notes.front: What is a simplified directional facility (SDF)?
notes.back: A facility giving a final approach course similar to an ILS localizer, with no glide slope information.
notes.explanation: The technique for flying it is essentially that of a localizer approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-10 “Simplified Directional Facility (SDF)”
notes.evidence: The SDF provides a final approach course similar to that of the ILS localizer. It does not provide glide slope information.
notes.example: Like a basic localizer with a wider beam and no promise that it points straight down the runway.

notes.front: What is area navigation (RNAV)?
notes.back: A method of navigation that permits aircraft operations on any desired flight path.
notes.explanation: Routes built on it are RNAV routes, usable by suitably equipped aircraft.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 “General definitions” (eCFR)
notes.evidence: Area navigation (RNAV) is a method of navigation that permits aircraft operations on any desired flight path.
notes.example: Like walking across a park by the direct line on your phone map instead of keeping to the paths between lamp-posts.

notes.front: What is required navigation performance (RNP)?
notes.back: A form of performance-based navigation that includes onboard performance monitoring and alerting, such as RAIM.
notes.explanation: The manual names RNAV and RNP as the two main categories of performance-based navigation.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-1 “General”
notes.evidence: RNP is a PBN system that includes onboard performance monitoring and alerting capability (for example, Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM)).
notes.example: Like a sat-nav that not only shows the route but beeps when it can no longer trust its own position.

notes.front: In which frequency band do VORs operate, and what limits their range?
notes.back: 108.0 to 117.95 MHz; they are line-of-sight, so range grows with the receiver’s altitude.
notes.explanation: So the lower the receiver, the shorter the usable range.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-3 “VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)”
notes.evidence: They are subject to line-of-sight restrictions, and the range varies proportionally to the altitude of the receiving equipment.

notes.front: Flying low in a valley, you lose a VOR that you received clearly at your cruising altitude. What is the most likely reason?
notes.back: C: VOR signals are line-of-sight.
notes.choices:
A) The VOR has been switched off for maintenance
B) Your receiver has failed
C) VOR signals are line-of-sight, and range falls with lower altitude
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing suggests an outage, and it worked moments before at a higher level. B: a receiver fault is less likely than a known line-of-sight limit.
notes.explanation: VOR range varies with the receiver’s altitude, so descending behind terrain can lose the signal.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-3 “VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)”
notes.evidence: They are subject to line-of-sight restrictions, and the range varies proportionally to the altitude of the receiving equipment.

notes.front: What is the only positive way to identify a VOR?
notes.back: Its Morse code identification, or its recorded automatic voice identification ending in the word “VOR”.
notes.explanation: The manual warns never to rely on voice transmissions from the flight service station that operates it, since one station may run several VORs.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-3 “VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)”
notes.evidence: The only positive method of identifying a VOR is by its Morse Code identification or by the recorded automatic voice identification which is always indicated by use of the word “VOR” following the range's name.

notes.front: You tune a VOR and hear a controller mention the station by name, but no Morse code. Your receiver only shows the database identifier. Is the VOR positively identified?
notes.back: C: no; you need the Morse or automatic voice ident.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the controller named it
B) Yes: the receiver shows its identifier
C) No: you need the Morse code or the automatic voice identification
notes.choicesExplained: A: identification should never rest on voice transmissions from a facility. B: a database identifier is only the expected one, not a decoded one.
notes.explanation: The manual names only the Morse code or the recorded automatic voice identification as positive.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-3 “VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)”
notes.evidence: The only positive method of identifying a VOR is by its Morse Code identification or by the recorded automatic voice identification

notes.front: What does it mean when a navigation aid’s identification has been removed?
notes.back: The facility is officially off the air for tune-up or repair and may be unreliable, even if signals are received.
notes.explanation: During maintenance a VOR may instead send a T-E-S-T code.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-11 “NAVAID Identifier Removal During Maintenance”
notes.evidence: Removal of identification serves as a warning to pilots that the facility is officially off the air for tune-up or repair and may be unreliable even though intermittent or constant signals are received.

notes.front: On the approach frequency the needles look normal but there is no identification at all. What do you do?
notes.back: C: treat it as unreliable and do not use it.
notes.choices:
A) Use it only for the final segment
B) Use it, since the needles look normal
C) Treat the facility as unreliable and do not use it
notes.choicesExplained: B and A: signals can still be received while a facility is off the air, so good-looking needles prove nothing.
notes.explanation: A missing identification is the warning that the facility may be off the air for repair.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-11 “NAVAID Identifier Removal During Maintenance”
notes.evidence: Removal of identification serves as a warning to pilots that the facility is officially off the air for tune-up or repair and may be unreliable even though intermittent or constant signals are received.

notes.front: What are the three original standard service volume classes for VOR and DME?
notes.back: Terminal (T), Low (L) and High (H).
notes.explanation: The usable distance of each class depends on altitude above the transmitter.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-8 “Navigational Aid (NAVAID) Service Volumes”
notes.evidence: The three original SSVs are shown in FIG 1-1-1 and are designated with three classes of NAVAIDs: Terminal (T), Low (L), and High (H).

notes.front: What happens if you set the OBS to the reciprocal of your intended course?
notes.back: The CDI shows reverse sensing: to correct, you must turn away from the needle.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s fix is simply to set the VOR to agree with the intended course.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Intercepting Lead Radials”, PDF p. 257
notes.evidence: If the VOR is set to the reciprocal of the intended course, the

notes.front: Tracking inbound to a VOR on the 090 radial (course 270°), you have set the OBS to 090 and the needle seems to work backwards. What should you do?
notes.back: C: set the OBS to 270, the course you are flying.
notes.choices:
A) Keep 090 and turn toward the needle
B) Keep 090 and ignore the needle
C) Set the OBS to 270, the course you are flying
notes.choicesExplained: A: with the reciprocal set, turning toward the needle takes you further off course. B: the needle is still useful once the OBS matches the course.
notes.explanation: Setting the VOR to agree with the intended course removes reverse sensing.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Intercepting Lead Radials”, PDF p. 257
notes.evidence: situation, set the VOR to agree with the intended course.

notes.front: In the handbook’s VOR intercept method, how is the intercept angle found, and within what limits?
notes.back: Double the difference between the radial to intercept and the radial you are on; not less than 20° nor more than 90°.
notes.explanation: The handbook then turns to that heading and holds it until the CDI centres.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Intercepting Lead Radials”, PDF p. 257
notes.evidence: 2. Double the difference to determine the interception angle, which will not be less than 20° nor greater

notes.front: You are on the 250 radial and must intercept the 280 radial outbound. Using the handbook’s method, what intercept heading do you fly?
notes.back: 340°: the difference is 30°, doubled to 60°, added to 280°.
notes.explanation: The same steps as the handbook: difference, doubled within 20° to 90°, then applied to the course.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Intercepting Lead Radials”, PDF p. 257
notes.evidence: 2. Double the difference to determine the interception angle, which will not be less than 20° nor greater

notes.front: Near a VOR, what shows impending station passage, and what confirms it?
notes.back: Rapid or fluctuating needle movement shows it is near; the TO/FROM indicator confirms positive station passage.
notes.explanation: The CDI fluctuates in the cone of confusion above the station, so the flag change is the reliable cue.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Common Errors”, PDF p. 259
notes.evidence: FROM indicator to determine positive station passage.

notes.front: Is DME distance the horizontal distance to the station?
notes.back: No: it is slant-range distance.
notes.explanation: DME times a signal round trip along the straight line to the station, which includes the aircraft’s height.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-7 “Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)”
notes.evidence: Distance information received from DME equipment is SLANT RANGE distance and not actual horizontal distance.

notes.front: You cross directly over a VOR/DME at about 6,000 feet above the station. Roughly what does the DME show?
notes.back: C: about 1 NM.
notes.choices:
A) 0.0 NM
B) It shows a warning flag
C) About 1 NM
notes.choicesExplained: A: slant range includes height, so it cannot read zero overhead. B: nothing about crossing the station makes DME flag.
notes.explanation: Directly overhead, slant range equals height, and 6,000 feet is roughly one nautical mile.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-7 “Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)”
notes.evidence: Distance information received from DME equipment is SLANT RANGE distance and not actual horizontal distance.

notes.front: Up to what distance may DME signals be received, and how accurate are they?
notes.back: Up to 199 NM at line-of-sight altitude; better than ½ mile or 3 percent of distance, whichever is greater.
notes.explanation: DME works on the line-of-sight principle, so height matters for reception.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-7 “Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)”
notes.evidence: Reliable signals may be received at distances up to 199 NM at line-of-sight altitude with an accuracy of better than 1/2 mile or 3 percent of the distance, whichever is greater.

notes.front: Your DME shows 12 NM while you track straight toward the station at 3,000 feet. Is that close to the ground distance?
notes.back: A: yes, it is close.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: far out and low, slant range is close to horizontal distance
B) No: it is always about 3 NM too long
C) No: DME shows ground distance only overhead
notes.choicesExplained: B: the error is not a fixed amount; it grows with altitude and closeness. C: overhead is where slant range differs most from ground distance.
notes.explanation: The slant-range difference increases with altitude and proximity, so far out and low it is small.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: This difference increases with aircraft altitude and proximity to the NAVAID.

notes.front: When turning onto a DME arc, how much lead is satisfactory at groundspeeds of 150 knots or less?
notes.back: About 0.5 NM.
notes.explanation: Faster aircraft need a proportionately greater lead.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “DME Arc”, PDF p. 260
notes.evidence: 2. A 0.5 NM lead is satisfactory for groundspeeds of

notes.front: As a guide on a DME arc, how much should you change the relative bearing for each half-mile off the arc?
notes.explanation: For example, half a mile to a mile outside the arc with the pointer on the wingtip, turn 20° toward the facility.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “DME Arc”, PDF p. 261
notes.evidence: RB 10°– 20° for each half-mile deviation from the desired arc.

notes.front: Flying a 12 DME arc clockwise around a station with the station off your right wing, the DME reads 12.6 and rising. What do you do?
notes.back: A: turn toward the station.
notes.choices:
A) Turn right, toward the station, and let the pointer move ahead of the wingtip
B) Turn left, away from the station
C) Hold heading; the arc will come back
notes.choicesExplained: B: turning away takes you further outside the arc. C: holding heading keeps the range increasing.
notes.explanation: Outside the arc, the handbook turns the aircraft toward the facility, about 10° to 20° of bearing change per half mile.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “DME Arc”, PDF p. 261
notes.evidence: RB 10°– 20° for each half-mile deviation from the desired arc.

notes.front: Why should you monitor an NDB’s identification continuously while using it?
notes.back: ADF receivers have no flag to warn of erroneous bearings.
notes.explanation: Disturbances that upset the bearing, such as lightning or precipitation static, also affect the identification.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-2 “Nondirectional Radio Beacon (NDB)”
notes.evidence: Since ADF receivers do not have a “flag” to warn the pilot when erroneous bearing information is being displayed, the pilot should continuously monitor the NDB's identification.

notes.front: With a fixed-card ADF, how do you find the magnetic bearing to the station?
notes.back: Magnetic heading plus relative bearing equals magnetic bearing to the station.
notes.explanation: The fixed card always reads zero at the top, so the needle gives only the bearing relative to the nose.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Automatic Direction Finder (ADF)”, PDF p. 247
notes.evidence: (MH + RB = MB to the station.)

notes.front: Under the ILS rule in section 91.175(k), what are the basic components of an ILS?
notes.back: The localizer, glide slope and outer marker (plus an inner marker when installed for Category II or III).
notes.explanation: The rule also lists substitutes for the outer marker, such as a compass locator or a DME fix in the procedure.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 (k) “Takeoff and landing under IFR” (eCFR)
notes.evidence: The basic components of an ILS are the localizer, glide slope, and outer marker, and, when installed for use with Category II or Category III instrument approach procedures, an inner marker.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The outer marker on your ILS is out of service. What are two things 91.175(k) allows as a substitute?
notes.back: Two of: a compass locator; precision approach or airport surveillance radar; a DME, VOR or NDB fix in the procedure.
notes.explanation: The rule lists these as acceptable replacements; a suitable RNAV fix in the procedure is another.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.175 (k) “Takeoff and landing under IFR” (eCFR)
notes.evidence: The following means may be used to substitute for the outer marker: Compass locator; precision approach radar (PAR) or airport surveillance radar (ASR); DME, VOR, or nondirectional beacon fixes authorized in the standard instrument approach procedure;

notes.front: The localizer operates on one of 40 ILS channels in which frequency range?
notes.explanation: The SDF uses the same 108.10 to 111.95 MHz range.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: The localizer transmitter operates on one of 40 ILS channels within the frequency range of 108.10 to 111.95 MHz.

notes.front: The localizer is adjusted for a full-scale course width of {{c1::700 feet}} at the runway threshold.
notes.explanation: Full scale means from full fly-left to full fly-right, so the needle is very sensitive close in.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: It is adjusted for a course width of (full scale fly-left to a full scale fly-right) of 700 feet at the runway threshold.

notes.front: Two miles from the threshold on the localizer, the needle is half deflected. Compared with the same deflection 15 miles out, are you further or closer to the centreline?
notes.back: A: closer to the centreline.
notes.choices:
A) Closer: the course narrows to 700 feet full scale at the threshold
B) The same: localizer deflection is linear
C) Further: the needle is less sensitive close in
notes.choicesExplained: C: sensitivity increases near the runway, not decreases. B: the localizer is an angular course that narrows toward the runway.
notes.explanation: With the full-scale width set at 700 feet at the threshold, the same deflection covers less distance close in.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: It is adjusted for a course width of (full scale fly-left to a full scale fly-right) of 700 feet at the runway threshold.

notes.front: Flying inbound on a localizer back course without reverse-sensing equipment, which way do you correct?
notes.back: Away from the needle deflection.
notes.explanation: The same “flying away from the needle” applies when outbound on the front course.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: when flying inbound on the back course it is necessary to steer the aircraft in the direction opposite the needle deflection when making corrections from off-course to on-course.

notes.front: On a localizer back course approach, what should you do with glide slope indications?
notes.back: Disregard them, unless a glide slope is specified on the approach chart.
notes.explanation: False glide slope signals near the back course can even make the glide slope flag disappear.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: Disregard all glide slope signal indications when making a localizer back course approach unless a glide slope is specified on the approach and landing chart.

notes.front: The glide path is normally set to {{c1::3°}} above horizontal.
notes.explanation: At that angle it crosses the middle marker at about 200 feet and the outer marker at about 1,400 feet above the runway.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: The glide path projection angle is normally adjusted to 3 degrees above horizontal so that it intersects the MM at about 200 feet and the OM at about 1,400 feet above the runway elevation.

notes.front: May you rely on glide path indications alone below the lowest authorised decision height?
notes.back: No: below it they must be supplemented by visual reference to the runway environment.
notes.explanation: The glide path may not be suitable for navigation below that height.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: any reference to glidepath indications below that height must be supplemented by visual reference to the runway environment.

notes.front: On a 3° ILS glide path you pass the outer marker. About how high above the runway should you be?
notes.back: About 1,400 feet.
notes.explanation: The manual says the 3° path crosses the outer marker at about 1,400 feet, a cross-check that you are on the real glide path.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: The glide path projection angle is normally adjusted to 3 degrees above horizontal so that it intersects the MM at about 200 feet and the OM at about 1,400 feet above the runway elevation.

notes.front: How can you avoid capturing a false glide slope?
notes.back: Fly the approach at the charted altitudes, capturing the glide slope from below.
notes.explanation: Intercepting from above raises both the risk of an unstabilised approach and of capturing a false course.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook Addendum B “False Courses” (November 2019), replacing “ILS Errors”
notes.evidence: Note that, if the approach is conducted at the altitudes specified on the appropriate approach chart (GS captured from below), these false courses are not encountered.

notes.front: What does an outer marker (or a suitable substitute) identify?
notes.back: The final approach fix for non-precision operations, such as a localizer-only approach.
notes.explanation: Markers are now used mainly for this; a middle marker is no longer required.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: An OM or suitable substitute identifies the Final Approach Fix (FAF) for nonprecision approach (NPA) operations (for example, localizer only);

notes.front: Where is a middle marker, where one remains?
notes.back: About 3,500 feet from the landing threshold, where the glide path is about 200 feet above the touchdown zone.
notes.explanation: Middle markers are no longer required and are not being installed at new ILS sites.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: The MM indicates a position approximately 3,500 feet from the landing threshold.

notes.front: What does an inner marker indicate, where installed?
notes.back: The point at which an aircraft on the glide path is at decision height on a Category II ILS approach.
notes.explanation: It is only required for Category II operations without a published radio altitude minimum.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-9 “Instrument Landing System (ILS)”
notes.evidence: An IM, where installed, indicates the point at which an aircraft is at decision height on the glide path during a Category II ILS approach.

notes.front: LDA versus SDF: which usually gives the more precise approach course, and which may be offset from the runway?
notes.back: The LDA is usually more precise; both may be offset (the LDA is never aligned, and the SDF may not be).
notes.explanation: Neither is part of a complete ILS, and the SDF’s course may be wider.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-10 “Simplified Directional Facility (SDF)”
notes.evidence: except the SDF course may not be aligned with the runway and the course may be wider, resulting in less precision.

notes.front: How many GPS satellites does a receiver need for an accurate three-dimensional position?
notes.back: At least four.
notes.explanation: The constellation is designed so that at least five are always visible worldwide.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: A minimum of four satellites is necessary for receivers to establish an accurate three-dimensional position.

notes.front: Your IFR panel GPS is un-augmented. Before filing a route that relies on it, what else must be installed and working?
notes.back: B: an approved alternate means of navigation.
notes.choices:
A) A second hand-held GPS
B) An approved alternate means of navigation for the route, such as a VOR receiver
C) Nothing, if the database is current
notes.choicesExplained: A: hand-held units are not approved for IFR navigation. C: a current database does not replace the required alternate means.
notes.explanation: The manual requires un-augmented GPS users under IFR to carry an alternate approved means suitable for the route.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Aircraft using un-augmented GPS (TSO-C129() or TSO-C196()) for navigation under IFR must be equipped with an alternate approved and operational means of navigation suitable for navigating the proposed route of flight.

notes.front: What does RAIM do?
notes.back: The GPS receiver checks its own integrity, making sure the available satellite signals meet the requirements for the phase of flight.
notes.explanation: Without RAIM the pilot has no assurance that the GPS position is sound.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: RAIM is the capability of a GPS receiver to perform integrity monitoring on itself by ensuring available satellite signals meet the integrity requirements for a given phase of flight.

notes.front: How many satellites does RAIM need to detect an integrity problem?
notes.back: At least 5, or 4 plus barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding).
notes.explanation: RAIM needs at least one satellite more than navigation itself needs.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: RAIM requires a minimum of 5 satellites, or 4 satellites and barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding), to detect an integrity anomaly.

notes.front: Your receiver has four good satellites and no baro-aiding. Can it navigate, and can it perform RAIM?
notes.back: C: it can navigate, but not perform RAIM.
notes.choices:
A) It can do both
B) It can do neither
C) It can navigate but cannot perform RAIM
notes.choicesExplained: A: RAIM needs a fifth satellite or baro-aiding. B: four satellites are enough for a three-dimensional position.
notes.explanation: Navigation needs four satellites; RAIM needs one more, or baro-aiding in place of it.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: RAIM requires a minimum of 5 satellites, or 4 satellites and barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding), to detect an integrity anomaly.

notes.front: What are two ways a pilot can get a RAIM prediction before flight?
notes.back: A manufacturer-supplied RAIM prediction tool; the FAA’s prediction website (or a flight service briefing).
notes.explanation: Satellite positions keep changing, so past experience at an airport does not guarantee RAIM next time.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Civilian pilots may obtain GPS RAIM availability information for nonprecision approach procedures by using a manufacturer-supplied RAIM prediction tool, or using the Service Availability Prediction Tool (SAPT) on the FAA en route and terminal RAIM prediction website.

notes.front: If RAIM is predicted not to be available, what are your options?
notes.back: Use another type of navigation and approach system, choose another route or destination, or delay until RAIM is predicted.
notes.explanation: On longer flights the manual also suggests rechecking the destination prediction en route.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: If RAIM is not available, use another type of navigation and approach system; select another route or destination; or delay the trip until RAIM is predicted to be available on arrival.

notes.front: Your preflight check predicts a RAIM outage at your arrival time, and the only approach at the destination is GPS-based. What is an acceptable plan?
notes.back: A: delay, or plan another destination or approach.
notes.choices:
A) Delay the flight until RAIM is predicted on arrival, or plan another destination or approach
B) Fly the approach without RAIM, watching the moving map
C) Go anyway; RAIM usually comes back
notes.choicesExplained: C: the prediction is the warning; the manual gives options, not hope. B: without RAIM there is no assurance of position integrity.
notes.explanation: These are the manual’s options when RAIM is not available.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: If RAIM is not available, use another type of navigation and approach system; select another route or destination; or delay the trip until RAIM is predicted to be available on arrival.

notes.front: On a GPS approach, how does full-scale CDI sensitivity change from 2 NM before the final approach waypoint?
notes.back: It smoothly changes from ±1 NM to ±0.3 NM at the final approach waypoint.
notes.explanation: The approach mode becomes active within 2 NM, so both RAIM and CDI switch to approach sensitivity.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Beginning 2 NM prior to the FAWP, the full scale CDI sensitivity will smoothly change from ±1 NM to ±0.3 NM at the FAWP.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Intercepting a GPS final course 1.5 NM before the final approach waypoint, you see the CDI deflection growing although your heading is a good intercept. Why?
notes.back: C: CDI sensitivity is increasing.
notes.choices:
A) A crosswind has pushed you off course
B) The receiver has lost RAIM
C) Sensitivity is increasing from ±1 NM to ±0.3 NM
notes.choicesExplained: B: loss of RAIM gives an alert, not a growing needle. A: the manual notes this impression arises even on an acceptable intercept heading.
notes.explanation: The manual warns that increasing sensitivity can make it look as if you are moving away from the course; cross-track error helps.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: with the CDI not centered, the corresponding increase in CDI displacement may give the impression that the aircraft is moving further away from the intended course even though it is on an acceptable intercept heading.

notes.front: Why did the FAA develop WAAS?
notes.back: To improve the accuracy, integrity and availability of GPS signals.
notes.explanation: It lets GPS be used from take-off through approach, including approaches with vertical guidance.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-18 “Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)”
notes.evidence: The FAA developed the WAAS to improve the accuracy, integrity and availability of GPS signals.

notes.front: A NOTAM says WAAS may not be available at your destination, but on the approach your WAAS avionics show vertical guidance available. May you use it?
notes.back: C: yes, at the level of service displayed.
notes.choices:
A) No: the NOTAM forbids vertical guidance
B) Only if ATC approves
C) Yes, using the level of service the avionics display
notes.choicesExplained: A: the manual calls these NOTAMs predictive, for planning. B: ATC approval is not the condition the manual sets.
notes.explanation: If an outage happens during the approach, you revert to lateral-only minima or another approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-18 “Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)”
notes.evidence: NOTAMs are predictive in nature and published for flight planning purposes.

notes.front: What does the manual ask of pilots about GPS jamming and spoofing?
notes.back: Closely monitor equipment for anomalies, promptly tell ATC of any GPS degradation, and be prepared to operate without GPS.
notes.explanation: GPS signals are low-strength and many aircraft systems depend on them.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-4 “Recognizing, Mitigating, and Adapting to GPS Jamming and/or Spoofing”
notes.evidence: pilots must place additional emphasis on closely monitoring aircraft equipment performance for any anomalies and promptly inform Air Traffic Control (ATC) of any apparent GPS degradation. Pilots should also be prepared to operate without GPS navigation systems.

notes.front: En route, your GPS position suddenly jumps several miles and the VOR needle disagrees with the moving map. What does the manual expect?
notes.back: B: tell ATC and use another navigation source.
notes.choices:
A) Keep following the GPS; it is more accurate than VOR
B) Tell ATC of the GPS problem and navigate by another source
C) Switch everything off and on again, then carry on
notes.choicesExplained: A: an anomaly is exactly when GPS may be wrong. C: a reset does not deal with interference outside the aircraft.
notes.explanation: Pilots meeting navigation errors should move to another source and request amended clearances as needed.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Pilots encountering navigation error events should transition to another source of navigation and request amended clearances from ATC as necessary.

notes.front: In a navigation specification such as RNAV 1 or RNP 1, what does the number mean?
notes.back: The lateral navigation accuracy in nautical miles, to be achieved at least 95 percent of the flight time.
notes.explanation: RNAV 1, for example, needs a total system error of no more than 1 NM for 95 percent of the time.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-1 “General”
notes.evidence: the numerical designation refers to the lateral navigation accuracy in nautical miles which is expected to be achieved at least 95 percent of the flight time

notes.front: An aircraft’s navigator meets 1 NM accuracy but has no onboard performance monitoring and alerting. Is it an RNAV or an RNP system?
notes.back: RNAV: RNP needs onboard performance monitoring and alerting.
notes.explanation: Both are categories of performance-based navigation; alerting is the difference.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-1 “General”
notes.evidence: RNP is a PBN system that includes onboard performance monitoring and alerting capability

notes.front: May a suitable RNAV system substitute for a VOR, DME or NDB that is out of service?
notes.back: Yes: as a substitute means of navigation, for example to hold over an out-of-service NDB.
notes.explanation: The same applies when the aircraft has no ADF or DME, or its ADF or DME is not working.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-3 “Use of Suitable Area Navigation (RNAV) Systems on Conventional Procedures and Routes”
notes.evidence: For example, if equipped with a suitable RNAV system, a pilot may hold over an out-of-service NDB.

notes.front: May a suitable RNAV system be used for lateral navigation on a localizer course without raw localizer data?
notes.back: No: localizer-based courses, including back courses, are excluded.
notes.explanation: The substitution allowances cover VOR, DME, NDB and similar facilities, but not localizer guidance.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-3 “Use of Suitable Area Navigation (RNAV) Systems on Conventional Procedures and Routes”
notes.evidence: These operations do not include lateral navigation on localizer-based courses (including localizer back-course guidance) without reference to raw localizer data.

notes.front: Your ADF has failed and the arrival requires an NDB fix and holding over the NDB. You have a suitable IFR GPS. What does the manual allow?
notes.back: C: use the GPS to identify the fix and hold.
notes.choices:
A) Use the GPS, but only if the NDB is also out of service
B) Nothing: an ADF is required
C) Use the GPS to identify the fix and hold over the NDB
notes.choicesExplained: B: the allowances apply even when a chart says “ADF required”. A: substitution also covers an aircraft whose ADF is not working.
notes.explanation: A suitable RNAV system may substitute when the aircraft’s ADF is not operational.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-3 “Use of Suitable Area Navigation (RNAV) Systems on Conventional Procedures and Routes”
notes.evidence: an aircraft is not equipped with an Automatic Direction Finder (ADF) or DME; or the installed ADF or DME on an aircraft is not operational.

notes.front: Fly-by versus fly-over waypoint: when does the turn start?
notes.back: Fly-by: before reaching the waypoint (turn anticipation). Fly-over: only after passing over it.
notes.explanation: RNAV procedures make use of both fly-over and fly-by waypoints.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 2, para 1-2-1 “General”
notes.evidence: Fly-by waypoints are used when an aircraft should begin a turn to the next course prior to reaching the waypoint separating the two route segments. This is known as turn anticipation.
